Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

This is an impressive manuscript that integrates across sub-disciplines in biology and shows compelling results regarding the adaptive evolution of an integrated domain. I detail my two major critiques below, both having to do with the framing of the results.

Overall, I found the interpretation and discussion around the evolutionary analysis to be lacking. The authors observe that the inferred ancient integrated domain alleles have low affinity for AVR-PikD. From this they conclude that the domain has recently evolved to recognize an effector different from its ancestral target. But what about recognition of ancient AVR-PikD? How do the authors eliminate this possibility? In an arms-race model, the null expectation would be that the NLR and effector would both change over time continuously (and perhaps indefinitely). The paper would benefit substantially from a more in-depth exploration/discussion of how the current results inform on what is already known of coevolution between NLRs and effectors.

Lastly, the manuscript is very dense with many experiments and analyses. Only a fraction of these analyses are important to the major inclusions of the manuscript in its current state, and I would encourage the authors to reduce the content of the manuscript substantially for future submissions. In this same vein, I found myself wondering whether this should be two manuscripts-one studying the molecular evolution of the NLR locus and the other a structure-function analysis of the important residues for recognition. Because the paper contains so many different types of data, and so much data, the authors often don't explore their results in detail nor their interpretation. Overall, I liked the paper but found that the paper did not offer a great deal of novel insight into the evolution of NLR-effector interactions. Perhaps with greater focus, the novelty of the findings will become clearer.

results.result: Pik-1 and Pik-2 orthologues are widely distributed across grass species. Phylogenetic analysis of CC-NLRs revealed that Pik-1 and Pik-2 sequences form two phylogenetically unrelated but well-supported clades, with representatives detected in distantly related grass species including members of the Pooideae and Panicoideae subfamilies, as well as across the Oryzoideae subfamily.
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C52 are well-supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 1 and supplementary figures. The ML phylogenetic trees based on NB-ARC domain sequences provide clear evidence for the widespread distribution and phylogenetic relationships of Pik orthologues across grass species.

results.result: The reference genome of O. brachyantha contains a truncated Pik-2 gene with a 46 bp deletion, but full-length ObPik-2 genes without this deletion are present in the O. brachyantha population. Genotyping of 16 additional O. brachyantha accessions identified six full-length ObPik-2 genes lacking the deletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C46 are supported by sequence analysis and genotyping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The identification of full-length genes in multiple accessions demonstrates that the deletion in the reference genome is not representative of the species.

results.result: Pik gene copy number varies across grass subfamilies. The majority of Oryzinae species contain single copies of Pik-1 and Pik-2 per accession, while Pooideae and Panicoideae members frequently encode multiple paralogues, with wheat carrying up to 9 Pik-1 and 10 Pik-2 genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are supported by phylogenetic analysis and gene identification data presented in Figure 1. The copy number variation is clearly documented across species, though the evolutionary mechanisms underlying this variation require further investigation.

results.result: Pik genes from the Oryza genus form two subclades corresponding to N-type and K-type haplotypes. These haplotypes have been maintained through speciation and coexist in different Oryza species.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 are supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and cited literature. The phylogenetic evidence clearly demonstrates the maintenance of both haplotypes across Oryza speciation events.

results.result: Pik-1 and Pik-2 genes are predominantly genetically linked in a head-to-head orientation across grass species. In 14 out of 15 species where both genes are present, at least one Pik pair shows this arrangement. Despite variation in intergenic region length (from ~2 kb in O. nivara to ~48 Mb in wheat), the genes exhibit largely conserved gene models with characteristic intron patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are well-supported by examination of genetic loci shown in Figure 1B and supplementary data. The conservation of gene structure and linkage across diverse species is clearly documented, though the functional significance of intergenic length variation remains to be explored.

results.result: Genetically linked Pik-1 and Pik-2 genes show strong positive correlation of synonymous substitution rates (R² = 0.87, p=0.95), significantly higher than expected by chance. This indicates the Pik-1/Pik-2 pair became genetically linked before the emergence of Oryzinae and prior to the BOP/PACMAD split (100-50 MYA).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by dS rate analysis shown in Figure 1C and statistical validation in Figure 1—figure supplement 5. The correlation analysis provides strong evidence for ancient genetic linkage, though the precise timing estimate relies on cited divergence dates that carry inherent uncertainty.

results.result: HMA-containing Pik-1 genes cluster into a single well-supported clade (the Pik-1 integration clade). All members carry the HMA domain in the same position between the CC and NB-ARC domains and feature an intron within the HMA, indicating derivation from a single integration event.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1A and gene structure analysis in Figure 1B. The conserved position and structure of the HMA domain across the clade provides strong evidence for a single integration event, though independent integrations followed by convergent evolution cannot be completely excluded.

results.result: The HMA integration in Pik-1 predates Oryza genus speciation and likely occurred before Oryzinae speciation (~15 MYA). All Oryza Pik-1 orthologues carry the HMA domain, and L. perrieri Pik-1 carries ~15 amino acids characteristic of the HMA integration site, suggesting the fusion occurred before Oryzinae speciation and was subsequently lost in L. perrieri.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by sequence analysis across Oryza species and examination of L. perrieri sequences shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The presence of partial HMA sequence in L. perrieri provides evidence for ancient integration followed by loss, though alternative scenarios cannot be completely ruled out.

results.result: The vast majority of Pik-1 genes from Pooideae and Panicoideae subfamilies lack the HMA domain, with only one of nine wheat Pik-1 paralogues carrying an HMA integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 are supported by examination of Pik-1 sequences from these subfamilies. The data clearly show the HMA domain is largely absent outside Oryzinae, though the evolutionary history of the wheat HMA-containing paralogue (introgression vs. ancient integration) remains uncertain.

results.result: The integrated HMA domain exhibits marked signatures of positive selection. In 96 out of 115 pairwise comparisons, dN > dS (ω ranging 0-2.45 for K-type and 1.13-3.50 for N-type), while only 9 out of 115 NB-ARC domain comparisons showed dN > dS (all with dS = 0, making ω calculations inconclusive).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are well-supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 2A-D. The contrast between HMA and NB-ARC domains is clear, though the inconclusive NB-ARC comparisons (dS = 0) limit the strength of the comparison. The elevated dN/dS ratios in the HMA domain provide strong evidence for positive selection.

results.result: Approximately 26% of HMA amino acid sites likely experienced positive selection based on likelihood ratio tests and posterior probabilities from ML codon substitution models.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 is supported by ML codon substitution model analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, C. Multiple models (M2, M3, M8) converge on evidence for positive selection at specific sites, though the exact percentage depends on model assumptions and posterior probability thresholds.

results.result: Reconstructed ancestral HMA variants exhibit a range of association strengths with AVR-PikD, but in every case the association is weaker than with present-day Pikp-HMA. This indicates binding strength has likely changed over the evolutionary history of Pikp-HMA.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The consistent pattern of weaker ancestral binding across multiple reconstructed variants provides strong evidence for evolutionary change in binding affinity, though the semi-quantitative nature of co-IP limits precise quantification.

results.result: Among four chimeric HMA constructs tested, only Pikp-1:ancHMALVKIE associated with AVR-PikD at levels similar to wild-type Pikp-1. This indicates the polymorphic residues in the IAQVV/LVKIE region are critical for evolution of enhanced AVR-PikD binding in Pikp-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C78 and C79 are supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The chimera swap approach provides clear evidence that the LVKIE region is necessary and sufficient for high-affinity binding, though the experiments do not exclude contributions from other regions in the native context.

results.result: SPR experiments reveal a binding hierarchy among ancHMA mutants, with ancHMALVKIE showing the strongest interaction (similar to Pikp-HMA), followed by ancHMALAKIE, then weaker binders. The two most recent mutations (Ala-222-Val and Val-230-Glu, collectively AV-VE) determined the HMA transition towards high-affinity AVR-PikD binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 are well-supported by SPR experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B. The quantitative binding data clearly demonstrate the hierarchy and identify AV-VE as critical mutations. Statistical analysis (Tukey's HSD, p<0.01) supports the significance of differences between mutants.

results.result: The AV-VE polymorphisms are unique to Pikp-1 and Pikh-1 among 19 integrated HMA sequences examined. Pikp-1 and Pikh-1 are highly similar, differing by only three polymorphisms including one synonymous substitution across nearly 3500 bp. The near-absence of synonymous polymorphisms suggests very recent emergence of the AV-VE polymorphisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by sequence comparison data. The low synonymous substitution rate provides strong evidence for recent divergence, though the inability to rigorously estimate divergence times (acknowledged by authors) limits precise dating of the AV-VE emergence.

results.result: The AV-VE substitutions are sufficient to increase binding affinity towards AVR-PikD independently of the other three polymorphic residues in the IAQVV/LVKIE interface, as demonstrated by the ancHMAIVQVE mutant.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5. The ancHMAIVQVE mutant (bypassing intermediate mutations) shows enhanced binding, demonstrating sufficiency of AV-VE. However, the authors acknowledge they cannot exclude quantitative epistatic effects that co-IP cannot detect.

results.result: All Pikp-1:ancHMA variants are autoactive and trigger spontaneous cell death in the absence of effector, requiring Pikp-2 for this activity. The PMASDKH/AMEGNND region (in β1–α1 and α2–β4 loops) underpins Pikp-1:ancHMA autoactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by HR cell death assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1-4. The consistent autoactivity across ancHMA variants and loss of autoactivity with AMEGNND mutations provides clear evidence, though the molecular mechanism underlying autoactivity remains to be elucidated.

results.result: In effector-dependent HR assays with autoactivity-suppressed mutants (AMEGNND background), binding strength directly correlates with HR strength. Pikp-1:ancHMALVKIE* triggered cell death at levels similar to Pikp-1, ancHMALAKIE* showed slightly reduced HR, while ancHMA*, ancHMALAKVV*, and ancHMALAQVV* did not elicit cell death above background. This indicates adaptive mutations in the IAQVV/LVKIE region enable both high-affinity binding and effector-dependent immune response activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are well-supported by HR cell death assays shown in Figure 6B, C and statistical analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 5. The correlation between binding affinity (from SPR) and HR phenotypes provides strong evidence linking molecular binding to functional immune response. Statistical analysis using besthr confirms significance of differences.

results.result: Among five Pikm-1:ancHMA chimeras tested, only Pikm-1:ancHMAEMVKE associated with AVR-PikD. This indicates Pikm-HMA evolved towards AVR-PikD association through mutations in the MKANK/EMVKE region, a distinct interface from the IAQVV/LVKIE region of Pikp-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C94 and C95 are supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2. The chimera approach clearly identifies EMVKE as the critical region for Pikm-1 binding, demonstrating a distinct evolutionary path from Pikp-1. One chimera (VH) was unstable, limiting interpretation.

results.result: SPR experiments reveal ancHMAEMVKE displays the highest interaction rates with AVR-PikD, followed by ancHMAEMANK and ancHMAMKANK. Despite similar binding at high concentration (400 nM), the mutants show marked differences in sensorgram shapes and off-rates. The ANK-VKE substitutions are essential for Pikm-HMA high-affinity binding of AVR-PikD.
results.evaluation: Claims C96 and C97 are supported by SPR experiments shown in Figure 8C, D and Figure 8—figure supplement 4, 5. The binding hierarchy is clear, though the authors note different stoichiometry (1:1 vs 2:1) for constructs with C-terminal extension, complicating direct comparison. The sensorgram shapes provide additional evidence for differential binding kinetics beyond simple affinity.

results.result: The ANK-VKE substitutions are present in three closely related Pik-1 alleles: Pik*-1, Pikm-1, and Piks-1. Pikm-1 differs from Piks-1 and Pik*-1 by only two and eight amino acid polymorphisms respectively, with no synonymous changes. This lack of synonymous changes demonstrates very recent emergence of these alleles and their associated ANK-VKE substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by sequence comparison data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1J. The absence of synonymous substitutions provides strong evidence for recent emergence, consistent with evolution during rice domestication, though precise dating is not possible.

results.result: The MKANK/EMVKE and IAQVV/LVKIE regions map to two of three previously described AVR-PikD binding interfaces. Structural analysis reveals V230E enhances interaction through hydrogen bonding with His-46. In both Pikm-HMA and Pikp-HMA, K262 is a major binding determinant, but its position is structurally shifted in Pikm-HMA, causing backbone conformational differences. N262K and K263E of the ANK-VKE substitution likely determine differential binding between ancestral and present-day Pikm-HMA.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 9 and crystal structure of ancHMALVKIE–AVR-PikD complex (1.32 Å resolution). The structural data clearly show the molecular basis for enhanced binding, though homology modeling of ancHMA (vs. experimental structure) introduces some uncertainty. The structural shift in K262 position between Pikm-HMA and Pikp-HMA is well-documented.

results.result: The HMA domain integrated into Pik-1 before Oryzinae speciation over 15 million years ago and has been under diversifying selection throughout its evolutionary history.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, and C66 together establish the timing and selective pressures on HMA integration. Phylogenetic evidence (C2, C66) combined with selection analysis (C3) provide converging lines of evidence. The 15 MYA date relies on cited literature for Oryzinae speciation timing, which carries inherent uncertainty in molecular clock estimates.

results.result: Two Pik-1 allelic variants (Pikp-1 and Pikm-1) independently evolved from a weakly binding ancestral state to high-affinity binding of AVR-PikD through distinct biochemical paths. For most of its evolutionary history, the Pik-1 HMA domain did not sense AVR-PikD, with recognition being a recent adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 represent the central conclusion of the manuscript, integrating ancestral sequence reconstruction, binding studies, and evolutionary analysis. The evidence from multiple experimental approaches (co-IP, SPR, HR assays) across both Pikp-1 and Pikm-1 lineages strongly supports convergent evolution. The weak ancestral binding and recent emergence of high-affinity variants are well-documented, though the identity of ancestral effector targets remains unknown.
